t:
The sentence below contains errors. Select the option with the correct use of tenses.
I will revised my course at least three times before my final examination.
o: I would revised my course at least three times before my final examination.
I will be revised my course at least three times since my final examination.
I will have revised my course at least three times before my final examination.
I must revised my course at least three times before my final examination.
e:
The original sentence has a grammatical error in the verb form "will revised" (should be "will revise"). Additionally, the context suggests an action completed before a future event (the final examination), which requires the future perfect tense ("will have revised").
• Option 1: "I would revised" is incorrect because "would" is used for hypothetical situations, and "revised" should be "revise" after "would."
• Option 2: "I will be revised" is incorrect because "revised" is passive, implying the course revises itself, and "since" is inappropriate for a future event.
• Option 3: "I will have revised" correctly uses the future perfect tense to indicate the action of revising will be completed before the examination.
• Option 4: "I must revised" is incorrect because "must" is a modal verb requiring the base form "revise."
Thus, the correct option is 3) I will have revised my course at least three times before my final examination.

e:

t: Select the option with the correct use of past tense.
o: The ancient Roman aqueducts was engineered to transport water over very long distances.
The ancient Roman aqueducts were engineered to transport water over very long distances.
The ancient Roman aqueducts were engineer to transport water over very long distances.
The ancient Roman aqueducts had engineered to transport water over very long distances.
e: The correct option is b). This sentence correctly uses the passive voice of the simple past tense ("were engineered"). The passive is required because the subject ("aqueducts") is the receiver of the action (engineered). The plural subject "aqueducts" correctly pairs with the plural verb "were." · Option (a): This has a subject-verb agreement error. The plural subject "aqueducts" requires the plural verb "were," not the singular verb "was." · Option (c): This is grammatically incorrect. The passive voice requires the past participle ("engineered"), not the base form "engineer." · Option (d): This is an incorrect passive construction. The past perfect passive would be "had been engineered." Note: Subject-Verb Agreement: Matching up singular or plural subjects with singular or plural forms of a verb is part of the process called agreement. This can be understood better by the examples given: - "She likes cooking." [singular subject and verb] -- "They like to cook vegetables." [plural subject and verb] Active and Passive Voice: When the person doing the action is the subject, the sentence is said to be in active form/voice. When the subject is what the action is directed at, then the sentence is said to be in passive form/voice. For example: Active Voice: Rita and her friends performed a skit. Here 'Rita and her friends' (subject) perform the action. Passive Voice: A skit was performed by Rita and her friends. Here 'skit' is the subject (at which the action is directed).

t:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in the past tense form. 
He will study diligently for the final History exam.
o: He studies diligently for the final History exam.
He is studying diligently for the final History exam.
He will be studying diligently for the final History exam.
He had studied diligently for the final History exam.
e: The verb "will study" is in the future tense. To change it to the past tense, we need to consider the appropriate past tense form. Option (d) correctly changes the future tense "will study" to the past perfect tense "had studied." The past perfect tense is formed by using "had" + the past participle of the verb. In this case, the past participle of "study" is "studied." Hence, (d) is the correct answer. Note: Participle: A word formed from a verb (e.g. going, gone, being, been) and used as an adjective (e.g. working woman, burnt toast) or a noun (e.g. good breeding). In English, participles are also used to make compound verb forms (e.g. is going, has been). Consider the sentences given below: Dancing at the party, the women fell on the ground. Encouraged by her parents, Rita went on to pursue her passion. The highlighted word in the first sentence is of the form Verb + ing and is used as a present participle. It is used to denote an action that is going on or incomplete or imperfect. The highlighted word in the second sentence is of the form verb + ed. It is used as a past participle. It denotes the completed action or state of the thing spoken of. A past participle ends with the following: -ed, -d, -t, -en, or -n. One should take great care and never get confused between a gerund and a present participle. They use the same forms but perform different functions: a gerund is a verbal noun, while a present participle is a verbal adjective.

t: Select the option with the correct use of present tense.
o: The process of photosynthesis in plants is converting light energy into chemical energy to fuel growth.
The process of photosynthesis in plants have converted light energy into chemical energy to fuel growth.
The process of photosynthesis in plants converts light energy into chemical energy to fuel their growth.
The process of photosynthesis in plants convert light energy into chemical energy to fuel their growth.
e: The correct option is c). This sentence correctly uses the simple present tense ("converts"). This tense is used to state general truths, scientific facts, and permanent realities. Photosynthesis is a constant, universal scientific process. · Option (a): This uses the present continuous tense ("is converting"), which is for actions happening right now or temporary situations. A scientific fact is permanent, not temporary. · Option (b): This uses the present perfect tense ("have converted"), which describes a past action with a present result. This is incorrect for a timeless process. It also has a subject-verb agreement error ("process" (subject) is singular, so it should be followed by the singular verb "has", not the plural verb "have"). · Option (d): This has a subject-verb agreement error. The singular subject "The process" requires the singular verb form "converts" (with an -s), not the plural verb "convert." Note: Subject-Verb Agreement: Matching up singular or plural subjects with singular or plural forms of a verb is part of the process called agreement. This can be understood better by the examples given: - "She likes cooking." [singular subject and verb] -- "They like to cook vegetables." [plural subject and verb]

t:

A) I had visited Paris several times in the past.
B) I visited Paris several times in the past.
C) I was visiting Paris several times in the past.
D) I have visited Paris several times in the past.
o: C
B
A
D
e: The option that expresses the given sentence in present perfect tense is (d). The present perfect tense is used to indicate an action that was completed at an unspecified time in the past with a connection to the present. It is formed by using the following construct - "has/have + the past participle form (V3) of the main verb" (have visited). Only sentence D follows the correct structure of the present perfect tense. Hence, (d) is the correct answer. Note: V1 -> Base form/simple form of verb, V2 -> Past form of verb (-ed form or irregular verb), V3 -> Past participle form of verb (-ed, -d, -t, -en, or -n), V4 -> Continuous form of verb / Present participle form of verb (-ing form), V5 -> Third person singular (V1+ -es or -s).

t: Select the option with the correct use of the present tense.
o: The Earth is revolving around the Sun in an elliptical orbit.
The Earth revolves around the Sun in an elliptical orbit.
The Earth has revolved around the Sun in an elliptical orbit.
The Earth has been revolving around the Sun since an elliptical orbit.
e: The correct option is b) The Earth revolves around the Sun in an elliptical orbit. This sentence correctly uses the simple present tense (revolves). The simple present tense is used to state universal truths, scientific facts, and general habits that are always true. The fact that the Earth orbits the Sun is a universal truth. Let's look at why the other options are incorrect: · Option (a): This uses the present continuous tense ("is revolving"). This tense is used for actions happening right now or for temporary situations, not for permanent universal truths. · Option (c): This uses the present perfect tense ("has revolved"), which implies a recently completed action or an action with a result in the present. This is inappropriate for a timeless fact. · Option (d): This uses the present perfect continuous tense incorrectly. "Since" must be followed by a point in time, not a description of the orbit like "an elliptical orbit".

t: Select the option with the correct use of future tense.
o: If the weather forecast is accurate, it is going to snow heavily tomorrow.
If the weather forecast is accurate, it will have snowed heavily tomorrow.
If the weather forecast will be accurate, it is going to snow heavily tomorrow.
If the weather forecast is accurate, it will have been snowing heavily tomorrow.
e: The correct option is a) If the weather forecast is accurate, it is going to snow heavily tomorrow. This sentence is a Type 1 conditional sentence, used for real future possibilities. The structure is If + Simple Present, ... Simple Future. The phrase "is going to" is a common way to express the simple future, especially for predictions based on present evidence (the accurate forecast). Let's look at why the other options are incorrect: · Option (b): This uses the future perfect tense ("will have snowed"), which is incorrect. It would mean the snowing will be finished by some point tomorrow, which is not the intended meaning of a general prediction. · Option (c): This is incorrect because the 'if' clause in a Type 1 conditional must use the simple present tense ("is"), not the future tense ("will be"). · Option (d): This uses the future perfect continuous tense, which is incorrect as it describes the duration of an action up to a future point, not a simple prediction.

NOTE: Auxiliary verb: A verb that gives grammatical information that is not given by the main verb of a sentence. It supports the main verb. Auxiliary verbs help to form the various tenses, moods, and voices of other verbs. The principal ones are be, do, and have. Example: She will sing a song tomorrow. Here, 'will' is the auxiliary verb that supports the main verb 'sing'. In English, participles are also used to make compound verb forms (e.g. is going, has been). Consider the sentences given below: Dancing at the party, the women fell on the ground. Encouraged by her parents, Rita went on to pursue her passion. The highlighted word in the first sentence is of the form Verb + ing and is used as a present participle. It is used to denote an action that is going on or incomplete or imperfect. The highlighted word in the second sentence is of the form verb + ed. It is used as a past participle. It denotes the completed action or state of the thing spoken of. A past participle ends with the following: -ed, -d, -t, -en, or -n. One should take great care and never get confused between a gerund and a present participle. They use the same forms but perform different functions: a gerund is a verbal noun, while a present participle is a verbal adjective.

t: Select the option with the correct use of the past tense.
o: While I was studying for my exam, my phone rang loudly.
While I had been studying for my exam, my phone rang loudly.
While I studied for my exam, my phone had rung loudly.
While I was studying for my exam, my phone was ringing loudly.
e: The correct option is a) While I was studying for my exam, my phone rang loudly. This sentence correctly uses the past continuous tense (was studying) for a longer, background action and the simple past tense (rang) for a shorter, interrupting action. This is the standard structure for showing an interruption in the past. Let's look at why the other options are incorrect: · Option (b): This uses the past perfect continuous ("had been studying"), which is not necessary here as there is no earlier past action to refer to. · Option (c): This incorrectly uses the simple past ("studied") for the longer action and the past perfect ("had rung") for the interrupting action. · Option (d): This uses the past continuous for both actions ("was studying" and "was ringing"), which suggests two parallel, ongoing actions rather than one interrupting the other.
